lead: Channel capacity is the largest mutual information any input distribution can create for a given channel. It is the best error-free data rate the channel can support. For a band-limited channel with additive white Gaussian noise, the Shannon-Hartley law gives C = B log₂(1 + S/N) bits per second. That single number decides whether a telephone line, Wi-Fi link or satellite path can carry the rate we want. Link budgets, DSL planning and 5G design all start from it.
prereq: You need: Chapter 7.3 for mutual information I(X;Y), and Unit 1 for AWGN and noise power spectral density N₀.

blocks.text: Take a channel with input X and output Y. Mutual information I(X;Y) measures how much of the input uncertainty the output removes. Capacity is the largest value of I(X;Y) we can get by choosing the input probabilities p(x):
C = max over p(x) of I(X;Y)
blocks.where: C is capacity in bits per channel use; p(x) is the input probability distribution; the channel p(y|x) is fixed.

blocks.text: For a continuous band-limited channel with additive white Gaussian noise, this maximisation gives the Shannon-Hartley law:

blocks.where: C is capacity in bit/s; B is bandwidth in Hz; S is received signal power in W; N is noise power in the same bandwidth in W; S/N is a dimensionless power ratio.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call this result Shannon's channel capacity theorem or the Shannon-Hartley law. A decibel value is not a ratio. Convert first: S/N = 10^(SNR(dB)/10). For example, 30 dB means S/N = 10³ = 1000. Capacity per hertz is C/B = log₂(1 + S/N) bit/s/Hz; it says how many bits each hertz can carry.
For a binary symmetric channel (BSC), each bit flips with probability p, independent of other bits. The capacity is
C = 1 − H(p) bits per channel use
blocks.where: H(p) = −p log₂ p − (1−p) log₂(1−p) is the binary entropy function in bits; p is the bit-flip probability.

blocks.text: Equal input probabilities 0 and 1 reach this value. At p = 0 the channel is perfect, H(0)=0, so C=1. At p = 0.5 the output is independent of the input, H(0.5)=1, so C=0. At p = 1 every bit is inverted; the receiver can invert it back, so the channel is perfect again and C=1. This last point is a favourite trap. For a binary erasure channel with erasure probability p_e, the capacity is
C = 1 − p_e bits per channel use
blocks.where: p_e is the probability that a bit is erased, not flipped.

blocks.text: An erased bit is lost, so one clean bit per use is the most we can send. The derivation is in Chapter 7.3.

sections.h3: Limits, units and the Shannon limit

blocks.text: Keep the units straight. C = B log₂(1 + S/N) gives bits per second. The BSC formula gives bits per channel use. One channel use may carry several bits, so a rate in bits per second is bits per use multiplied by the number of uses per second. Mixing the two is an easy way to lose marks.
What happens as B grows without limit? Noise power is N = N₀B, where N₀ is the noise power spectral density in W/Hz. Substitute:
C = B log₂(1 + S/(N₀B)) → (S/N₀) log₂ e ≈ 1.44 S/N₀ bits/s
blocks.where: S is signal power in W; N₀ is noise power spectral density in W/Hz; e is 2.718...; the arrow means B tends to infinity.

blocks.text: So infinite bandwidth does not give infinite capacity; capacity saturates at about 1.44 S/N₀. A wider bandwidth admits more noise as well as more signal. For reliable communication, the energy per information bit is E_b. The Shannon limit is the smallest E_b/N₀ that can support arbitrarily small error probability as the rate tends to zero: about −1.6 dB. Practical codes aim near this line; Chapter 7.9 shows how close they get. Capacity is an upper bound, not a promise that a simple uncoded link will work.

figure.caption: Capacity per hertz against SNR in decibels. At high SNR each extra 3 dB adds about 1 bit/s/Hz; at low SNR the absolute changes are smaller.

examples.question: A telephone channel has bandwidth B = 3.1 kHz and SNR = 30 dB. (a) Find its capacity. (b) Repeat for SNR = 20 dB. (c) A BSC has bit-flip probability p = 0.01; find its capacity per channel use.
steps: For 30 dB, convert to a power ratio: S/N = 10^(30/10) = 10³ = 1000.
Use B = 3.1 kHz = 3100 Hz in the Shannon-Hartley law: C = 3100 log₂(1 + 1000) = 3100 log₂ 1001 bit/s.
C = 1 − H(0.01) = 1 − 0.0808 = 0.9192 bit per channel use.
examples.answer: The telephone channel capacity is about 30.9 kbit/s at 30 dB, about 20.6 kbit/s at 20 dB, and the BSC capacity is 0.919 bit per channel use.
examples.check:
import math
B = 3100.0
snr_db_30 = 30.0
snr_30 = 10 ** (snr_db_30 / 10)
C_30 = B * math.log2(1 + snr_30)
print(round(C_30 / 1000, 1))
snr_db_20 = 20.0
snr_20 = 10 ** (snr_db_20 / 10)
C_20 = B * math.log2(1 + snr_20)
print(round(C_20 / 1000, 1))
p = 0.01
H = -(p * math.log2(p) + (1 - p) * math.log2(1 - p))
C_bsc = 1 - H
print(round(C_bsc, 3))

traps: Putting the decibel value straight into log₂(1 + S/N). Convert with S/N = 10^(SNR(dB)/10) first.
Mixing bits per second with bits per channel use. Shannon-Hartley gives bit/s; the BSC and erasure formulas give bit/use.
Using a voltage ratio as S/N. S/N is a power ratio; if a voltage ratio is given, square it before the formula.
Saying capacity is zero at BSC p = 1. At p = 1 every bit is inverted, and the receiver can undo a known inversion, so C = 1.
Using B in kHz in the formula. Convert bandwidth to Hz so C comes out in bit/s.

quiz.q: State the Shannon-Hartley law and define each symbol.
quiz.a: C = B log₂(1 + S/N) bit/s. B is bandwidth in Hz, S is signal power in W, N is noise power in W, and S/N is a dimensionless power ratio.

quiz.q: Why is BSC capacity zero at p = 0.5 and one at p = 1?
quiz.a: At p = 0.5 the output is independent of the input, so mutual information is zero. At p = 1 every bit is inverted; a known inversion is undone by the receiver, so the channel carries one bit per use.

quiz.q: A channel has B = 4 kHz and SNR = 10 dB. Find C.
A BSC has p = 0.1. Find its capacity per channel use.
quiz.a: H(0.1) = −0.1 log₂ 0.1 − 0.9 log₂ 0.9 = 0.469 bits. C = 1 − 0.469 = 0.531 bit per channel use.

quiz.q: At fixed S and N₀, does C grow without limit as B tends to infinity? Explain.
quiz.a: No. N = N₀B grows with B, and C = B log₂(1 + S/(N₀B)) tends to (S/N₀) log₂ e ≈ 1.44 S/N₀ bit/s. Extra bandwidth brings extra noise.

quiz.q: Convert SNR = 17 dB to a power ratio.
A link has C = 20 kbit/s. A system uses 25 kbit/s with a strong code. Can it be reliable? Relate to the coding theorem.
quiz.a: No. A rate above capacity cannot be made reliable by any code; the coding theorem in Chapter 7.5 says reliable codes exist only below C.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern systems use LDPC, turbo and polar codes to come within a fraction of a decibel of the Shannon limit; 5G data channels use LDPC and control channels use polar codes. Research moves beyond infinite block length to finite-blocklength capacity, which is what short packets in machine-type communication actually face. Search next for “Shannon limit”, “AWGN channel capacity”, “finite blocklength” and “polar codes”.
